title: My Daily Brief
overview: This edition is dominated by the aftermath of Tuesday's midterm elections, in which Republicans lost control of both chambers of Congress: President Trump replaced chief of staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller, and voters' rejection of data center expansion rattled AI stocks from Wall Street to Seoul. Also covered: a stronger-than-expected October jobs report, the arrest of Meghan Markle's father on federal child sexual abuse material charges, Sen. Chris Murphy's stroke recovery, and several local and Asian business stories.

stories.headline: Trump names Stephen Miller White House chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles
stories.summary: President Trump announced Friday that longtime adviser Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, days after Republicans lost control of the House and Senate. Wiles submitted her resignation Thursday night and will move to Trump's political operation; Trump praised her work and said, "I wanted to make a change." A White House official called the decision "very amicable," while Axios sources described it as mutual but driven by the election results. Miller, currently deputy chief of staff and a key architect of the administration's immigration policies, starts Monday. Democrats, including House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, sharply criticized the pick.
key_facts: Miller, 41, takes over Monday; Wiles, 69, resigned Thursday night.
Wiles was the first woman to serve as White House chief of staff and served about 21 months, Trump's longest-serving chief across both terms.
Trump called Miller "one of my most trusted advisors"; Wiles said serving Trump "has been the honor of a lifetime."
Jeffries called Miller "a dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist" and urged Trump to "fire him today."

perspectives.framing: The Guardian framed the appointment as "extraordinary" and a sign of an aggressive fight with congressional Democrats, describing Miller as Trump's most controversial aide and detailing family separation, the travel ban, the "Hatemonger" biography, and a Democratic letter calling him a white nationalist; it quoted Chris Whipple and David Axelrod as critics. PBS (via AP) was more straightforward, focusing on Wiles's tenure, her cancer recovery and Miller's background.

Axios framed the move as replacing a moderating force with a maximalist one, signaling Trump may double down on policies that it said helped Republicans lose Congress. The Hill focused on Jeffries' denunciation.

Fox News emphasized Trump's and Wiles's warm statements, the "amicable" nature of the change, Wiles's history and cancer recovery, and quoted an administration official calling Miller "a great pick." The Washington Examiner described the move as a defiant, combative response to defeat, comparing it to Stalin's "Not one step back" order.

disputed: Whether Wiles left voluntarily: Fox's White House source called it "very amicable" and Axios sources said mutual, while The Guardian described her as "ousted."
How Miller will approach the incoming Democratic Congress; commentators predict confrontation, but this is speculation.
stories.why: The choice of chief of staff signals how the White House intends to deal with a newly Democratic Congress for the next two years.

stories.headline: Thomas Markle, Meghan's father, arrested on federal child sexual abuse material charge
stories.summary: Thomas Markle Sr., 82, father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, was arrested Friday at a senior living facility in Polk County, Florida, and charged with one count of possessing child sexual abuse material. Prosecutors say FBI agents seized about 78 items, including slides, negatives and books, from two Los Angeles-area storage units he rented since 2008, and allege some images show him with nude underage girls. The case follows claims reported by The Sun that his son, Thomas Markle Jr., found such images at his father's former home in the Philippines and reported them. Markle has previously called the allegations "sick lies"; he made an initial court appearance in Tampa Friday.
key_facts: Charge: one count of possession of child sexual abuse material; maximum 20 years in federal prison.
About 78 items seized from two LA-area storage units rented for roughly 18 years.
Prosecutor Bill Essayli said there was no evidence of US victims based on the seized material so far, and the investigation is ongoing.
Meghan said last month she was "deeply distressed" and that a letter with allegations about her father was sent to London police in 2018.

perspectives.framing: The Guardian and PBS (AP) gave detailed, measured accounts of the criminal complaint, prosecutors' statements, Meghan's statement, and noted Essayli's awareness of reports Markle may have dementia and his court-appointed lawyer's lack of comment.
DW, WSOC and BBC focused on the charges, evidence and official statements, with WSOC and BBC noting Markle's earlier denial calling the claims "sick lies."

The New York Post used vivid tabloid language ("alleged pedophile dad," "vile child porn case") and emphasized details of his arrest appearance, while also citing prosecutors' allegations and Meghan's statement.

disputed: Markle denies the allegations; the charges have not been proven.
Whether material found in the Philippines is part of the US case: the Post says his Philippines home was raided, while other outlets describe the federal case as based on the LA storage units.
Reports that Markle may have dementia, and how that affects the case.
stories.why: The case involves serious alleged crimes against children and a widely followed family connected to the British royal family.

stories.headline: Voters back data center limits; White House says AI build-out will continue
stories.summary: Voters supported restrictions on data center development in nearly all local ballot measures this election, and many winning Democratic candidates pledged tougher regulation. National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett said Friday he still expects data center growth to continue as projected, arguing near-term projects are unaffected and that welcoming states will keep building. Trump wrote that he is "100% in favor of Super Intelligence" and will work with states that want data centers. Meanwhile, OpenAI announced it would stop using non-disclosure agreements with public officials on data center projects, and incoming Democratic officials such as Wisconsin Gov.-elect David Crowley are weighing moratoriums and disclosure rules.
key_facts: Ballotpedia: majorities voted to restrict data centers in at least 46 of roughly 50 measures this year.
AdImpact: more than $380 million spent on TV ads mentioning data centers; Democrats outspent Republicans more than 3-to-1.
Data Center Watch: 32 of 34 winning governors support stronger regulation or restrictions; 12 support bans or moratoriums.
CNBC Voter Poll: 56% of voters called data centers a crucial or major issue.

perspectives.framing: The Verge and PBS (AP) emphasized a coming tougher regulatory environment, Democratic wins in data-center hot spots, concerns about water, power bills and the environment, and industry responses such as OpenAI dropping NDAs. AP noted data centers were not a top issue for most voters.
CNBC centered Hassett's optimistic White House view and linked Thursday's market plunge to political uncertainty; TechCrunch focused on what the outcome means for the tech industry.

The Daily Caller cast the results as a populist rebuke of "tech oligarchs" rather than a byproduct of the Democratic wave, highlighting cross-partisan opposition including 58% of Republicans and the industry's spending advantage.

disputed: Tallies differ slightly: TechCrunch says 40 of 41 Tuesday measures passed; Daily Caller says 46 of 47 decided; Ballotpedia via CNBC says at least 46 of about 50.
How important data centers were to voters: CNBC and Daily Caller cite polls ranking it highly, while AP says it was not a top issue for most voters.
Whether build-out will actually slow, as Hassett disputes.
stories.why: The fate of the data center boom affects electricity bills, local land and water use, and a major driver of US economic growth and stock markets.

stories.headline: US adds 165,000 jobs in October, beating forecasts
stories.summary: Employers added 165,000 jobs in October, nearly three times the roughly 59,000 economists expected, and unemployment edged down to 4.1% from 4.2%, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday. August and September were revised up by a combined 84,000 jobs. Wages rose 3.1% from a year earlier, still below recent inflation, and a broader underemployment measure rose. October's consumer price report is due Tuesday.
key_facts: Unemployment rate: 4.1%, down from 4.2%.
Professional and business services added 70,000 jobs; health care 42,000; transportation and warehousing 25,000; manufacturing 19,000.
U-6 underemployment rose from 7.6% to 7.9%; part-time for economic reasons rose by 339,000 to 4.8 million.
Average hourly earnings up 3.1% year over year; September inflation was 3.7%.

perspectives.framing: The Guardian highlighted labor-market resilience but stressed that wages trail inflation, the Iran war's effect on gas prices, Fed rate hikes and voter frustration with the economy expressed in the midterms.
WBTV and The Hill reported the numbers straightforwardly, with WBTV noting the rising U-6 rate and wages below inflation.

The Daily Caller called the report a welcome rebound but cited economists warning of persistent weakness, especially for entry-level workers and the long-term unemployed. Fox Business emphasized that the gains "blew past" expectations.

stories.why: The jobs data shapes Federal Reserve rate decisions and how households experience the economy amid high prices.

stories.headline: Sen. Chris Murphy leaves hospital after stroke, will miss several weeks of votes
stories.summary: Connecticut Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy, 53, said Friday he was discharged from Johns Hopkins Hospital after a small hemorrhagic stroke last Saturday and will spend several weeks at a rehabilitation center. He will miss Senate votes when Congress returns Monday. His doctor said he is expected to make a full recovery. Murphy is seen as a possible 2028 presidential candidate.
key_facts: Diagnosed with a small bleed in the thalamus region of the brain.
He called 911 after feeling unwell at his son's hockey game.
Johns Hopkins' Dr. Jose Suarez said a full recovery is expected after rehabilitation.

perspectives.framing: PBS (AP) reported his statement and placed it alongside other senators' strokes, including Lujan, Van Hollen and Fetterman.
CNBC and The Hill reported the medical details and his campaigning for Democrats before the election.
The Washington Examiner covered it similarly, noting his potential 2028 run and missed votes.

stories.why: Murphy's absence affects Senate votes during the lame-duck session and he is a prominent Democratic figure.

stories.headline: NCDOT reopens I-77 South community center as toll lanes project resumes
stories.summary: North Carolina transportation officials reopened a community engagement center on West Morehead Street for the $4.3 billion I-77 South toll lanes project in Charlotte. The project faced backlash for cutting into historically Black neighborhoods, and Charlotte City Council rejected it in May before reversing in September after the state promised $300 million in community benefits and threatened to seek repayment of nearly $70 million in design costs. Officials said they want to build trust, and Mayor Rob Harrington plans a working group to oversee promised spending.
key_facts: The project covers an 11-mile stretch from uptown to the South Carolina line.
The state promised $300 million for parks, grocery stores and a cap over part of the interstate.
Council member Malcolm Graham: "No one's going to be happy. I'm not happy as a council member."

perspectives.framing: WFAE detailed the opposition's concerns about displacement and whether tolls ease traffic, the state's financial pressure on local governments, and officials' pledges to deliver investments.
Queen City News highlighted residents' memories of I-77's original construction; WCNC focused on the mayor addressing public pushback.

disputed: Whether toll lanes will relieve congestion, as opponents dispute.
Whether promised community investments will be delivered.
stories.why: The project will reshape a major Charlotte commuter corridor and nearby historically Black neighborhoods.

stories.headline: Kospi falls 6% as AI sell-off spreads to Asia
stories.summary: South Korea's Kospi closed down 6.02% Friday at 5,059.69 after an intraday drop of 8.78% triggered a circuit breaker, following an overnight AI and chip sell-off on Wall Street. The Korea Herald attributed the slide to fears of tighter US data center regulation after the midterms; Samsung Electronics and SK hynix fell to seven-month lows. Japan's Nikkei and Taiwan's market also fell sharply. Some Korean analysts called the regulatory fears overblown.
key_facts: Kospi briefly fell below 5,000 for the first time since Feb. 6.
Samsung fell 6.35%; SK hynix fell 10.44%.
Kospi is at roughly 55% of its June 22 peak of 9,114.55.
Foreign investors were net sellers of 2.77 trillion won.

perspectives.framing: The Korea Herald detailed the market damage and quoted analysts arguing fears of an AI investment collapse are excessive.
Fox Business briefly reported the regional plunge, emphasizing the trading halt and AI stock selling.

disputed: Analysts dispute how much US regulation will actually slow AI investment; one estimated a 15–30% probability of new project suspensions in Texas, Georgia and Ohio.
stories.why: The sell-off shows how US political shifts on AI infrastructure ripple through global markets and chipmakers.

stories.headline: Novant Health paychecks delayed by payroll tech issue
stories.summary: Thousands of Novant Health employees, including in the Charlotte area, reported missing direct deposits Friday. The health system blamed a technical issue with its new payroll distributor, apologized, and said payments would arrive by end of day. It said it would reimburse employees for any problems caused.
key_facts: Cause attributed to a new payroll distributor.
Novant said paychecks would arrive Friday and it would reimburse affected staff.

perspectives.framing: WSOC and WCNC reported employee complaints and Novant's explanation and apology.

stories.why: Novant is a major regional employer, and delayed pay can cause real hardship for workers.

stories.headline: Korean crypto exchange GOPAX halts withdrawals and trading after hacking threat
stories.summary: South Korean cryptocurrency exchange GOPAX suspended withdrawals, deposits and trading Friday as a precaution after receiving an email from a group claiming to have hacked it. The exchange moved most hot-wallet assets to offline cold wallets and canceled outstanding orders. It said it has not verified the threat and no losses have been reported.
key_facts: Withdrawals halted at 2:55 p.m.; trading suspended around 3:53 p.m.
Regulators earlier confirmed cybersecurity incidents at 37 financial institutions affecting about 470,000 customer records.

perspectives.framing: Yonhap and The Korea Herald reported the company's statements and placed it within a series of recent financial-sector cyber incidents.

disputed: Whether the hacking claim is genuine is unverified.
When services will resume was not stated.
stories.why: Exchange users cannot access their assets, and the incident adds to concerns about cybersecurity in Korean finance.

stories.headline: Chery recalls 53,882 cars over rear-axle welding defect
stories.summary: Chinese automaker Chery will recall 53,882 Tiggo 5x and Omoda vehicles built between June 2022 and December 2023 over a rear-axle welding defect, China's market regulator said. In extreme cases the defect could cause loss of wheel control. Chery's chair has apologized over quality issues after a rear axle detachment involving an Omoda in Malaysia.
key_facts: 53,882 vehicles affected; recall starts later this month.
Models: Tiggo 5x and Omoda produced June 2022–December 2023.

perspectives.framing: The Korea Herald (Reuters-Yonhap) reported the regulatory filing and the Malaysia incident.

stories.why: The recall raises safety and quality questions for a fast-growing Chinese automaker selling abroad.

investigations.question: What is happening with AI regulation in the US and EU?
investigations.update: On the US side, the midterms point toward tighter AI data center regulation: voters approved restrictions in nearly all local ballot measures, and most winning governors back stronger rules, with some supporting moratoriums. The BBC reports that fears of more AI regulation appear to have triggered an AI stock selloff, though concerns about the industry had been building. The White House, via Kevin Hassett and Trump, says it still backs continued build-out, and AP notes Trump may stall any federal crackdown. OpenAI dropped NDAs with public officials, and a bipartisan permitting bill in the lame-duck Congress could limit oversight of new data centers. None of today's articles address EU AI regulation.
